cases.title: From a CAD assembly to a bill of materials in the ERP, in one click
cases.impact: Took a manual, error-prone transfer between engineering and the ERP and made it automatic, validated and about 6× faster end to end.
cases.summary: A Windows application for a manufacturing plant that reads the real assembly structure from SolidWorks and PDM, normalizes it, validates it and loads the bill of materials into the plant's ERP, then emails the team exactly what changed.

metrics.label: Saving ~200 BOM rows to the ERP
Automated flow per assembly, all stages

beforeAfter.label: BOM capture in the ERP
beforeAfter.before: Typed row by row from Excel
beforeAfter.after: Automatic, with a check after every write

beforeAfter.label: Telling the team what changed
beforeAfter.after: Generated: new, updated and removed parts

beforeAfter.label: Setting up a new PC
beforeAfter.after: Copy the folder and open it

cases.problem: Every machine engineering designs is a SolidWorks assembly with dozens or hundreds of parts. Purchasing, warehouse and production need that structure as a bill of materials in the ERP. That step was manual: review each part, copy it to Excel, fix duplicates by hand, type it into the ERP and write an email describing the changes. It was slow, error-prone and left no trace of what had changed.
context: The plant already runs SolidWorks with PDM, a Pervasive (Actian) database behind the ERP and SQL Server behind PDM. Replacing any of them was out of scope.
Each workstation had the PDM vault in a different path and its own configuration.
Users keep their own SolidWorks session open; the tool must never interfere with it.
A bad write to the ERP is expensive to undo, so correctness comes before speed.
cases.approach: A layered desktop app. A C# .NET 8 engine drives SolidWorks through COM and returns a canonical ledger of every document with its identity and version. Python services normalize parts, apply engineering's duplicate rule, complete material and stock size, and pass three quality gates before anything is written. Writes to the ERP are batched and verified afterwards; the change email compares against what was already in the ERP.

decisions.why: Every run writes a candidate first. Only when the CAD structure, enrichment and ERP-readiness gates all pass is it promoted to final. If something fails, the screen shows the exact cause and nothing is written.
decisions.alternative: Best-effort export with manual review afterwards, which is how errors reached the ERP before.

decisions.why: Each stage logs machine, version, status and duration to a shared table. The 5-minute save turned out to be unindexed lookups caused by driver padding; batched preloads of 200 parts and exact-key queries cut each lookup from 0.14–0.36 s to 2–27 ms without removing a single verification.
decisions.alternative: Guessing at bottlenecks or dropping the post-write checks to save time.

decisions.choice: Never touch the user's SolidWorks session
decisions.why: The engine only closes processes it started: it checks PIDs against pre-existing ones, holds an exclusive mutex and fails closed if it cannot enumerate processes.
decisions.alternative: Reusing or killing whatever SolidWorks instance is open, which risks losing someone's work.

decisions.choice: No passwords handed out per machine
decisions.why: Only access to a shared database travels with the build. ERP and PDM credentials are fetched on first run and stored encrypted with Windows DPAPI at machine level, so rotating one updates every station.
decisions.alternative: Config files with credentials on each PC.

implemented: Guided flow: Search → Generate → Save → Email, with the ERP target always visible.
PDM vault discovery from the Windows registry on any PC and path.
C# CAD engine with a canonical ledger (part number, configuration, document ID, version).
Batched ERP writes for structure, new parts and inventory, each verified afterwards.
Automatic change email: new, updated and removed against the ERP.
A second workspace for logistics: material catalog, densities and current prices.
evidence: 1,737 automated tests with pytest; CAD and PDM end-to-end tests run on a dedicated machine.
Stage timings measured on real assemblies before and after each optimization.
Atomic failure reports per run, so a blocked run always explains itself.
About 179k lines of Python (tests included) and 14k of C#.
next: Keep a warm SolidWorks instance between runs to cut startup time, tested on one PC first.
Split the largest UI controllers into smaller modules.
cases.learned: Speed came from measuring, not guessing. Every second we gained was found in a timing table, and none of it came from removing a validation.

cases.plain: Think of it as a translator between the people who design machines and the people who buy and build them. Engineers draw a machine on the computer; this system reads that drawing, lists every screw and plate it needs, checks the list and loads it into the company's purchasing system. What took about 9 minutes of careful copying per machine now takes about a minute and a half, and the system refuses to save anything that does not check out.
steps: The engineer types the machine's code
The system reads the 3D design and lists every part
It checks the list and stops if anything is missing
It loads the list into the ERP and emails what changed

cases.title: A commercial CRM from first contact to after-sales

status.label: In operation · WhatsApp channel in pilot

cases.impact: Gave a B2B installation business one traceable flow from lead to quote, project and warranty, with web leads arriving automatically and no quote leaving without a person's review.
cases.summary: A Next.js and Prisma CRM that connects prospects, a guided quote builder, a price catalog, projects, installations and warranties, plus an authenticated web-to-CRM intake that is idempotent by design.

metrics.label: Guided quote: client, solution, line items, review
Quotes sent without human review, by rule
Retries of the same web form never create a second lead

cases.problem: The business sells and installs projects. Leads, quotes, installations and warranties lived in different places, and website forms had to reach the sales team without duplicates and without anything automatic ever sending a price to a customer.
context: Website form providers retry deliveries, so the same submission can arrive more than once.
Quotes combine catalog prices, material multipliers and installation; they must stay under a salesperson's control.
Different roles see different things: sales, operations and administrators.
Deleting a prospect affects quotes, projects and warranties, so it must be deliberate and audited.
cases.approach: Model the commercial chain explicitly (prospect → quote → project → warranty) on a relational schema with Prisma. Web leads enter through a dedicated webhook that authenticates, validates, normalizes and deduplicates, marks the origin as WEB and stops at human review.

decisions.why: Forms, integrations and the chat flow can register and organize opportunities, but a quote is always prepared, reviewed and sent by an authorized person.
decisions.alternative: Auto-generated quotes from form data, fast but risky for pricing and reputation.

decisions.choice: Idempotent web intake keyed on an event ID
decisions.why: A retried delivery finds the existing record and stops, so duplicates never reach the pipeline.
decisions.alternative: Plain inserts, which create a new lead on every retry.

decisions.choice: A deterministic chat flow before any generative AI
decisions.why: The WhatsApp module follows a rule-based conversation engine and is kept as a technical pilot, not presented as a production channel.

decisions.choice: Granular permissions and audited destructive actions
decisions.why: Roles start from templates and can be tuned per user. Cascade deletion requires permission, shows its impact, asks for confirmation and keeps the audit trail.
decisions.alternative: A single admin role and soft rules.

implemented: Dashboard with live indicators, alerts and upcoming actions.
Prospects with owner, status, estimated value and next action.
Guided 4-step quote builder with drafts, persistent folio, PDF and commercial states.
Price catalog with base prices, material multipliers and change history.
Projects and installations with owner, progress, risk and evidence; warranties and maintenance.
Users with role templates and per-user permissions; passwords hashed with scrypt.
evidence: Unit tests with Vitest for the quote calculator, authentication, web intake and conversation engine.
Lint, tests and build required before every change.
Running on the company's server; screenshots on this page come from a local copy with seed data.
next: Move WhatsApp to the official Business API before calling it a production channel.
cases.learned: The reliability of an integration is decided at its boundary. Once authentication, idempotency and the human-review rule were fixed there, the rest of the CRM could stay simple.

cases.title: Attendance and overtime, from biometric clocks to HR reports
cases.impact: Replaced manual handling of clock data with a synchronized database and rule-based overtime, so HR gets period reports in its own template instead of rebuilding them by hand.
cases.summary: A layered .NET 8 system that syncs employees and punches from ZKTeco clocks into SQL Server, interprets noisy in/out records, calculates hours and overtime by schedule and generates Excel and PDF reports for HR.

metrics.label: Projects in one .NET 8 solution, split by layer
Scheduled sync windows from the clocks
Reports in the company's own template

cases.problem: Attendance came from biometric clocks whose raw punches are noisy: entries recorded as exits, duplicates, missing marks. HR needed worked hours and authorized overtime per schedule, in its own report format, and some data had to reach the ERP database too.
context: Clock data is not trustworthy as-is; in/out modes are often inverted.
Overtime rules depend on each schedule and on per-employee authorization.
Reports must keep HR's existing Excel template.
Credentials and site settings must stay out of the repository.
cases.approach: A clean split into Domain, Application and Infrastructure, with a WinForms desktop for daily operation and a separate sync agent. Punches land in SQL Server with sync state; the attendance engine rebuilds shifts and applies schedule rules; reports render from the corporate template.

decisions.why: Reading the clocks runs on its own schedule and does not depend on someone having the desktop app open.
decisions.alternative: Syncing only when HR opens the app.

decisions.choice: Rules by schedule, not hard-coded hours
decisions.why: Overtime starts at different times per schedule and requires authorization per employee, so it lives in configuration.

decisions.choice: ERP mirror with preview and locks
decisions.why: Writing attendance into the ERP database is optional and always previewed first.

implemented: Employee and punch sync from ZKTeco clocks to SQL Server, with automatic schema bootstrap.
Shift reconstruction that handles inverted and noisy in/out records.
Worked hours and overtime with per-employee authorization and per-schedule rules.
Admin tools to edit employee data, review history and run syncs.
Excel and PDF reports from the corporate template; web and API layer with role policies in progress.
evidence: Executive report documenting the real scope in operation.
Feature flags allow rolling back a single module without stopping the platform.
Settings in versioned files are safe defaults; secrets live in local files and environment variables.
next: Finish parity between the web and desktop versions.
Analytics on attendance patterns for HR.
cases.learned: Hardware data needs an interpretation layer. Treating raw punches as facts would have pushed every clock error straight into payroll.

cases.plain: Fingerprint clocks record when people arrive and leave, but they make mistakes: an entry saved as an exit, a double punch. This system collects those records every few minutes, cleans them up, calculates hours and overtime according to each person's schedule, and hands HR the report in the format they already use.

The system fixes noisy punches and calculates overtime
HR gets the report in Excel or PDF

items.title: Quality management system (ISO 9001)
items.text: Electron, React and TypeScript on SQL Server, moved from SQLite with 18 versioned migrations and a data migration script. Document control with permissions, signatures, an audit log and workflow emails, plus a records engine where a new record type is configuration, not a new screen. Several modules are still interface prototypes; an internal readiness audit set the hardening plan before any production use.

items.title: Real-estate operations prototype
items.text: A hexagonal monorepo: domain, application and infrastructure packages with layer rules enforced by dependency-cruiser, 10 architecture decision records, money stored in integer cents, idempotent payments, 29 domain tests and Playwright end-to-end checks with axe. An honesty matrix separates what works, what is simulated and what is proposed.

items.title: Point of sale on Odoo Community
items.text: A modular layer over Odoo Community 19: mobile scanner with temporary pairing, hashed tokens, rate limiting and acknowledged events, and an authenticated owner PWA. Fiscal invoicing runs in simulation.

principles.title: Engineering habits that show up in every project.

items.title: Start from the process that exists
items.text: Understand the current workflow, its data and its constraints before proposing software.

items.title: Integrate before replacing
items.text: ERPs, CAD tools, legacy databases and files are part of the system. Connect them first.

items.title: Make state traceable
items.text: Roles, history and validation are features. If an auditor asks, the answer should be a query.

items.title: Automate with a person in the loop
items.text: Automate capture, calculation and follow-up. Keep sensitive decisions with people.

items.title: Report status honestly
items.text: Implemented, pilot and roadmap are different words. I use them precisely.
